title: Same note, different sound: the secret is in the overtones
body: A guitar and a piano can play the same note at the same volume and still sound different. That quality is called **timbre**, or tone colour. Most notes are not one pure frequency: they are the main note plus harmonics at 2, 3, 4… times its frequency, and the balance of their strengths is a major factor in each instrument’s sound. How a note starts and fades matters too.

slides.alt: Animation on a green oscilloscope: two waves with the same 440 Hz period but different shapes. Sine waves at 440, 880, 1320 Hz and up are added one by one as spectrum bars grow, two different mixes of the same harmonics make two shapes, and two notes with different envelopes follow.
slides.music: “Late Night Radio” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Play the pure tone. Then drag the harmonic bars or pick a recipe and play again. Try a mix with the 1× bar at zero.
slides.takeaway: Mixes of the same harmonics repeat 440 times a second, so they share one pitch; the harmonics’ strengths give each its colour. Without the 1× bar, 2× and 3× together still repeat 440 times a second.

slides.heading: The harmonic series
slides.text: Harmonics are whole-number multiples of the main note, the fundamental. An A at 440 Hz is really a combination of 440, 880, 1320, 1760 Hz and so on, heard as one note.

slides.heading: The first harmonics of an A at 440 Hz
slides.note: Evenly spaced harmonics blend into one note; their strengths shape its colour.

slides.question: In the sound of a transverse flute, which frequency is heard most strongly?
slides.explanation: A flute’s dominant frequency is double the fundamental: the 2nd harmonic. The dominant frequency is always a multiple of the fundamental, even when it isn’t the fundamental.

slides.prompt: Cut the first moment off a recorded piano or trumpet note. What happens?
slides.answer: It gets harder to tell which instrument it is
slides.detail: That start, the attack, is highly characteristic: the hammer hitting the strings, or the first blast of the player’s lips.

slides.heading: Same family, still different
slides.text: Timbre is also what lets you tell apart two instruments from the same family, like an oboe and a clarinet, even when they play the same note.
